title: B.C. restaurant group alleges $2.1M in missing staff tips, sues payment company executives
summary: A B.C.-based restaurant group that operates Moxie's, Chop Steakhouse and Shark Club is suing six current and former executives and directors of a digital payment company over more than $2.1 million…

image.caption: A civil lawsuit from B.C.'s Northland Restaurant Group is targeting payment firm XTM’s former directors after millions in employee tip funds allegedly went missing across B.C. (Sammy Kogan/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: British Columbia

A B.C.-based restaurant group that operates Moxie's, Chop Steakhouse and Shark Club is suing six current and former executives and directors of a digital payment company over more than $2.1 million in funds allegedly owed to the group.
Northland Restaurant Group alleges money intended for employee tips was not properly safeguarded

A B.C.-based restaurant group that operates Moxie's, Chop Steakhouse and Shark Club is suing several former executives and directors of a digital payment company over more than $2.1 million in funds allegedly owed to the group.

Northland Restaurant Group and several affiliated companies filed a notice of civil claim in B.C. Supreme Court on Nov. 10, alleging that Ontario-based XTM Inc. failed to properly safeguard money entrusted to it for distribution to restaurant employees.
XTM went bankrupt and obtained creditor protection in February following a substantial shortfall in client funds, according to the court filing.
An Ontario court subsequently approved the sale of most of its business assets, including its digital payment platform, to a Calgary-based fintech company.

Northland is now seeking to recover losses from six people who served as XTM's directors or senior executives. They are Keith McKenzie, Randy Khalaf, Olga Balanovskaya, Michael Li, Jakob Ripshtein and Cary Strange.

Northland alleges the defendants knew or should have known about the company's handling of client funds. It also alleges that they either assisted in breaches of trust or received money that should have been protected.
The allegations have not been proven in court.
The interior of a Shark Club Sports Bar and Grill in 2019. (Jackson Weaver/CBC)
How the payment system worked

According to the lawsuit, Northland entered into an agreement with XTM in August 2024 to use its digital payment platform — which at the time was known as AnyDay, now called GratiaPay — to distribute gratuities and petty cash reimbursements to employees working at restaurants.
Under the agreement described in the lawsuit, XTM was required to hold the deposited money separately from its own operating funds and use it only for payments to employees.
Any money that had not yet been transferred to employees' cards was supposed to remain Northland's property and be returned to the restaurant group upon request.
Missing tips leave some servers out of pocket
But Northland alleges XTM failed to follow those requirements.
The lawsuit says Northland learned on Jan. 30 that XTM had placed client money into a single pooled account rather than maintaining separate accounts as required.

blocks.text: According to the lawsuit, the account contained approximately $12 million belonging to about 4,000 clients, with Northland and its affiliates among the largest.
Northland alleges roughly 75 per cent of that money, approximately $9 million, was no longer available.
More than $2.1M allegedly owed
According to the court filing, XTM signed an acknowledgement of debt on Feb. 2, confirming it owed Northland $2,161,647.07 as of Jan. 30.
The amount represented money Northland had deposited with XTM that had not yet been loaded onto employees' prepaid cards.
The lawsuit alleges XTM's CEO, Marilyn Schaffer, also promised to make a $50,000 repayment but Northland did not receive the money.
A tipping jar is seen at a coffee shop in Toronto. The lawsuit alleges that XTM owes Northland more than $2.1 million. (Sammy Kogan/The Canadian Press)
Northland says its lawyers formally demanded repayment on Feb. 7, but XTM did not respond.

Later that month, XTM obtained creditor protection and some of its assets, including the payment program, were acquired by Pateno Payments. According to the civil claim, Northland and other clients have been able to continue using that payment platform.
Northland is asking the court to order the return of any such funds and award damages, including punitive damages as well as legal costs.
Restaurants had to pay out of own pockets
Ian Tostenson, president and CEO of the B.C. Restaurant and Foodservices Association, estimates that about 3,000 businesses and nearly 15,000 employees were affected by XTM's financial troubles.
He said restaurant operators stepped in to cover the missing funds, paying employees out of their own pockets to ensure they received their tips.
“They recognized it's an important part of their compensation and so … was replaced by the businesses,” he said. “I have yet to meet an employer that did not pay the money back to their employees.”

blocks.text: Tostenson said the case also highlights the need for restaurants to scrutinize third-party payment providers before trusting them with employee gratuities.
"In the case of XTM, we know these guys were around for quite a few years and so we didn't question their financial ability," he said.
"My advice to our industry is make sure you do a check out of any fintech company you want to do business with."
